verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are left replaying a single reply all day. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Your thoughts racing after that brief message are not a failure; they are the mind's natural turbulence. Notice the wind itself, and let the day carry on.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes a steady yogi who feels all beings as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. The verse names this difficulty honestly and sets up the answer that comes next. That brief reply has set your mind racing, and Arjuna names this exact restlessness as normal, not a personal failure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You are facing your first Diwali without your dad, and that emptiness is real. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Let this thought sit beside your grief today—the core of who your dad was was never ended by his body’s death, even as you light the diyas this year.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, where Arjuna is paralyzed by grief and refuses to fight. Krishna tells him that the self was never born and will never cease to be. It does not die when the body dies. The self simply outlasts every change that bodies go through, including birth, growth, decay and death. Your father's body has changed beyond recognition, yet the core of who he was was never ended by that death. That truth can sit beside your grief without rushing it away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
verse_text.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the self casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones, just as a person sets aside old clothes to put on new ones. You are carrying the weight of this first Diwali without your dad, and this image can offer a gentle picture of transition rather than finality. Rest in the self leaving a worn body behind, without letting this soften the size of what you have lost.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse_text.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body, and the steady person is not bewildered by this. You already know how much you have changed across the years while remaining you. Let that same continuity stand beneath you today, without shrinking the emptiness of this first Diwali without your dad.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: No weapon cuts it, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it.
verse_text.translation: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that no weapon cuts the self, no fire burns it, no water wets it, and no wind dries it. This means whatever happened to your dad’s body could not reach who he was. You can stand on this image of him as something untouched, even as you carry the weight of this first Diwali without him.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama that even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little. For you, this means keeping one brief thread to someone who steadies you, even in the isolation after your father’s first Diwali. Let that contact be as small as a single message or a quiet call.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
verse_text.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that he accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or a little water when offered with love. You could place a flower or a glass of water somewhere today as a small gesture from your heart. It gives your love a place to go without asking for anything in return.

story.title: Bharata returns to Ayodhya
story.summary: Bharata was far away at his grandfather's home when his father, King Dasharatha, died. Messengers called him back without telling him why. He rode into an Ayodhya that had gone quiet, went looking for his father, and learned he was gone. He fell to the ground and wept. When he could stand again, the family priest Vasishtha gently told him it was time to perform the last rites, and he did them, grieving as he went.
story.lesson: Missing the goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next.

days.reading: Bharata rode into Ayodhya to find his father already gone, and the priest gently told him it was time for the last rites. You are facing your first Diwali without your dad, and missing that goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next, perhaps by lighting a lamp in his memory today.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from the section mocking our failure to give up pleasures. He looks at the moth and the fish. The moth does not know the flame burns. The fish does not know the hook waits inside the bait. But we know the danger. We see how desires tangle us in a net of harm. And still we do not let go. He says this shows how deep delusion runs in us. You know the sweetness is costing you something. You still reach for it each day.

verse_text.speaker: Indra, disguised as a jackal
verse_text.setting: The jackal tells Kashyapa that getting more will not cure his discontent.
verse_text.line: Getting what you want doesn't satisfy. Craving grows like a fire fed with more wood.
verse_text.translation: There is no satisfaction in getting what you want. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes up more, like a fire fed with fuel.

days.reading: Bhishma, speaking through a jackal, says that getting what you want does not satisfy. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes higher, like a fire fed with fuel. This speaks to the restlessness you carry: each sweet you reach for only feeds the flame, leaving the wanting sharper than before.

verse_text.speaker: Yama
verse_text.setting: Nachiketa has refused wealth and long life; Yama begins teaching.
verse_text.line: The good and the pleasant both knock. The wise choose the good; the foolish grab the pleasant.
verse_text.translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them and tells them apart. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.

days.reading: Yama tells Nachiketa that the good and the pleasant both come to a person, and the wise examine them to tell them apart, choosing the good. You feel restless while studying, caught between what feels good right now and what is truly good. Pause and sift what arrives today, naming which is which before you grab it.

verse_text.speaker: Manki
verse_text.setting: Manki, after his last savings are lost in a freak accident, speaks to his own desire.
verse_text.line: Desire, I know your root: my own imagining. I'll stop feeding you, and you'll be gone.
verse_text.translation: Desire, I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all.

days.reading: Manki tells his own desire, 'I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone.' You keep promising yourself you will stop, yet the wanting returns daily. Today’s task is simply to notice the moment you start picturing the next sweet thing, and refuse to feed that picture.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
verse_text.translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a steady mind pulls its senses back from what pulls at them, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs. You could try one small tortoise move today when the wanting spikes: close the tab or put your phone face-down. Then notice the pull fade on its own.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse_text.line: When your mind drifts to harmful things, steer it back to good ones. That's the whole teaching.
verse_text.translation: When the mind has sunk into bad things, bring it down into good ones with effort. That is the summary of all the scriptures.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama: when the mind sinks into harmful things, steer it back to good ones with effort. You could notice when your attention drifts toward the next sweet thing, and then place it on one small task nearby. This is not about forcing away the restlessness, but gently guiding where your mind rests today.

story.title: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
story.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
story.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

days.reading: Manki watches his last money dangle from a camel’s neck as his young bulls die. After blaming fate, he turns to desire and names its root as his own imagining, refusing to feed it anymore. For you, this shows that the sweetness you reach for each day is born in the mind, and the story points to the moment you stop imagining that next fix.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You mentioned that zero discipline lately makes even small tasks feel like climbing a mountain. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. When your thoughts loop like this, the verse names the struggle honestly: a mind this stormy does not obey on command. You can rest in that recognition today, letting the image of the wind stand beside your own heavy tasks.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard about the highest yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna answers that practice and letting go can train it. Your mind is not failing you. It is simply stormy, and that storm makes small tasks feel like mountains right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You did not realise how much of your life was your closest friend until he moved abroad and your talks faded. Krishna tells Arjuna, see me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When the daily rhythm of that bond empties out, this can point to a connection that distance itself does not erase.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to settle the mind through meditation. He says that a person who sees the divine everywhere and sees every being resting within the divine will never be out of sight of the divine, and the divine will never lose sight of that person. The bond you thought was only with one person can also be felt as a wider presence that does not vanish when distance grows.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna where the divine is found.
verse_text.line: The divine lives in the heart of every being, yours included.
verse_text.translation: The Lord dwells in the heart of every being, Arjuna, moving all beings by his power as if mounted on a machine.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the divine dwells in the heart of every being, yours included. Because this presence is already inside you, in this flat and this city, you are not empty or without ground. You carry someone living within you, even where your closest friend now is far away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna who he is to every being.
verse_text.line: I am your goal, your support, your witness, your home, your shelter and your friend.
verse_text.translation: I am the goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the home, the refuge and the friend; the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house and the undying seed.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna, I am your goal, your support, your witness, your home, your shelter and your friend. With your closest friend far away, this verse names what stands beneath you: a support, a shelter and a friend who does good expecting nothing in return. You can rest your feet on that ground today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, briefly describing meditation and the peace it brings.
verse_text.line: The divine is the well-wisher of every being, you included. Knowing this, you find peace.
verse_text.translation: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that he is the selfless friend of every being, the one who receives all offerings and rules all worlds. You may feel unseen right now after your closest friend moved abroad and your daily life shifted. This verse offers the ground that someone already wishes you well without expecting anything back, giving you a steady place to stand in the quiet.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Feel others' joy and pain as if they were your own. That is the highest practice.
verse_text.translation: One who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere, Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, is considered the highest yogi.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to feel others' joy and pain as if they were his own; that is the highest practice. Since your closest friend moved abroad and your life feels empty, you could reach out to one person today and share a small update or ask how they are doing. This turns your focus outward, just as the verse suggests.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse_text.line: Hate no one. Be friendly and kind, free of 'mine' and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving.
verse_text.translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to hate no one, to be friendly and kind, free from possessiveness, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving. After your closest friend moved abroad, you could reach out to one person today with a simple, open message, letting go of any quiet resentment. That small step is the friendship Krishna describes, and it belongs to you right now.

story.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
story.summary: Ram had lost his home, and his wife Sita had been taken. Sugriva, driven out by his brother, had lost his home and his wife too. They met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Then Sugriva brought out the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away. Ram broke down at the sight of them, and Sugriva, who had his own grief, comforted him: in trouble, think it through steadily, and lean on your friend.
story.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

days.reading: Ram and Sugriva, each exiled and grieving, met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Seeing Sita’s dropped jewels, Ram broke down, and Sugriva, bearing his own loss, steadied him by leaning on their bond. In your empty feeling after your closest friend moved abroad, this shows two people in trouble can carry each other.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: Your best mate died in a car crash three weeks ago, and uni carries on like nothing happened. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Let this thought sit beside you today: what your friend most deeply was was not ended by the crash, even as the world around you keeps moving.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken by the thought of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the true self was never born and will never die. It does not perish when the body perishes. The self simply outlasts every change that bodies go through. Your friend is gone from this world, but what they most deeply were was not ended by the crash.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Your app crossing a million downloads shows real momentum. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is what the world follows. In this success, you can let your original dorm-room humility guide how you lead now, so the people around you take their cue from that groundedness.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just urged Arjuna to act for the good of the world. Now he explains why even those who have nothing left to gain still keep working. A respected person does something, and others copy that action. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows it. The idea is that people take their cue from those they look up to. So anyone with standing carries the weight of the example their conduct sets. You have reached a point where your work reaches many hands. The same rule applies to you now. The way you carry this success will quietly shape how your team and your family understand what matters.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: With your client demo tomorrow and everything already ready, you still fear something might break live. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. You are not failing at control; you are simply facing a mind that refuses to settle, and the Gita names that struggle honestly before offering a way through.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard about a steady mind that treats joy and pain as equal. Arjuna objects that such calm cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously. It names the difficulty before offering the way through practice and letting go. You are facing a mind that refuses to settle even when your demo is ready. The Gita names this struggle honestly before it offers the way through.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: Going back to work after five years at home brings a mix of nerves and excitement. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. Your hopeful energy for this new chapter is itself a real strength that can carry you through the first days back.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is drowning in grief after Sita has been taken. Every bird and mated deer around the water deepens his longing. Lakshmana steps in and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the root of every effort and the strongest resource a person has. Your hopeful energy for this new chapter is itself a real strength that can carry you through the first days back.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You carry a running list of what your baby has eaten, slept, and whether a rash is normal. The Yoga Vasishtha describes a mind caught in endless waves of 'done, doing, must do,' where the bird of thought faints tangled in reckonings. Your worry today is that same loop, not a failing of your care. When the next hour brings a new thought, let it land as a wave passing through, and return to the breath in your body right now.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, two men who grew up together in a forest hermitage and later spent years apart in hard austerities. Now they meet again as old men. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that he has not. He says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It never rests for a moment. Its depths dance with worry. The mind keeps saying this I have done, this I am doing, this I must do. Your hourly checks on your baby are part of that same endless wave. The verse names the loop, not your care.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You retired on Friday and want to begin this new chapter with intention. Lakshmana tells Ram that enthusiasm is powerful, and for the one who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. As you step into this fresh season, your own resolve can carry you through whatever lies ahead.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is sinking in grief after Sita is taken. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her, and his sorrow deepens. Lakshmana, Rama's younger brother, answers this long lament by saying that enthusiasm is powerful. There is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The point is that beauty can sharpen grief, yet a friend can remind you of your own strength. You have just stepped away from decades of work and want to meet this new chapter with clear intention. Lakshmana's words point to the energy of your own will as the resource that will carry you forward now.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: You are facing a shaky job where your salary did not come this month. Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. This verse names the same physical overwhelm you might feel right now, without judging it as weakness.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has asked to see the two armies lined up. He looks across and sees his teachers, uncles, sons and friends ready to fight and to die. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. His limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. The verse is his honest report of grief and fear taking over his body. It proposes that even the strongest people freeze. The teaching begins with a breakdown, not with a hero. You are facing a shaky job where your salary did not come this month. This verse names the same physical overwhelm you might feel right now, without judging it as weakness.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You reread a team reply you sent, wondering what it landed like. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. In that same breath, he names exactly the loop you are caught in. The wind does not obey the archer; it simply moves, and so does this thought, again and again.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing that a yogi sees all beings as equal. Arjuna says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to steady, but he answers that practice and letting go can train it. You are caught in the same loop Arjuna names, rereading a message you sent because the mind will not settle. The verse says this restlessness is real, and it points toward practice rather than forcing the thought away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
verse_text.translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.

story.title: Action with devotion: surrender
story.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
story.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: At every family dinner, you sit as the other one while your sister’s path shines ahead. Krishna tells Arjuna to raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self. You can choose to stop pushing yourself down in that seat and instead lift yourself up from within.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is caught between grief and duty. Krishna tells him that a person must lift themselves by their own effort. The self alone can be the friend of the self, or the enemy of the self. The choice depends on how one treats oneself.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: After every choice, you keep replaying whether you did wrong, and sleep has become hard. Krishna hears Arjuna say the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. You are not alone in this loop; the Gita takes the struggle seriously before offering a way through. Tonight, when the thoughts return, notice the breath moving like air—something you do not have to control, only rest beside.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last, because the mind is too restless. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously and answers that practice and letting go can train it. After a decision, you keep replaying whether you did wrong, and sleep has become hard. The Gita names this loop before it offers a way through.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: When the mind chases a wandering sense, it is swept off like a boat in the wind.
verse_text.translation: When the mind runs after the roving senses, it carries away one's understanding, as the wind carries a boat away on the water.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind chases a wandering sense, it is swept off like a boat in the wind. This means a single detail can pull your attention away and carry your understanding with it. Notice when your mind drifts after one thought, and gently bring it back to what is right in front of you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Like a lamp in a windless place that doesn't flicker: that's a settled mind.
verse_text.translation: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker: that is the image used for the yogi of controlled mind practising union with the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a settled mind is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker. You do not have to force your thoughts to stop; you simply let the flame keep its own light while the winds around it settle. Tonight, notice one moment when the room is quiet and let that steadiness be enough to rest in.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Little by little, with patience and steady resolve, settle the mind and let other thoughts go.
verse_text.translation: Little by little one should come to rest, with understanding held steady; fixing the mind on the self, one should think of nothing else.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to settle the mind little by little, with patience and steady resolve, letting other thoughts go. Your mind keeps replaying each decision and wondering if you chose wrong, making sleep hard to find. This does not ask you to force silence tonight; it simply points to a gradual resting, one small letting-go at a time.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Yes, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But practice and letting go can train it.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Undoubtedly, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to control. But it is held by practice and by detachment, Kaunteya.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the mind is indeed restless and hard to control. Yet it can be trained by steady practice and by loosening your grip on what it keeps chasing. You could try returning your attention to one simple task, then gently letting go when it wanders, again and again.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse_text.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to draw the restless mind back wherever it wanders, again and again. You could try noticing when your thoughts loop after a choice, then gently guiding attention back to your breath for a few seconds. Each return is simply the practice itself.

story.title: Pingala's song
story.summary: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

days.reading: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who stayed awake waiting for a lover who never came, only to realize her wakefulness came from her own hope for someone else to arrive. That insight let her drop the expectation and sleep peacefully. For you, the loop after every decision may work the same way: the replay keeps going because a part of you still waits for an outcome to settle the mind. Letting that waiting go can bring the rest the night has refused.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: Mummy ka dialysis hafte mein teen baar hota hai aur bachche bhi chhote hain, har din dar lagta hai. Krishna, far from home, tells Yashoda that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. Your own distance from home means you too may feel the ache of missing those small, tender things that only a mother gives. Hold on to the name you carry at home, and let that memory be real today.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He tells her to stay well and that he and his brother will return in a few days. He adds that since the day he left home, no one there has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya. He has also missed his morning breakfast and his evening warm milk. The verse proposes that missing home is itself a form of love. It shows that the one who has gone away still longs for the small tenderness of being known and fed by his mother. Your distance from your mother carries the same ache. The fear you feel each day is tied to missing those small, tender things that only she gives.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You are in a slow, happy season where the children are healthy and the garden is growing, and you want to savour it and go deeper. The poet wonders at the freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, good company, and learning whose only fruit is calm, asking what generous austerity ripened into this. Today, this sense of wonder can sit beside your care for your parents, letting the quiet dignity of this ordinary season simply be what it is.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to the reader from his Worship of Shiva. He has just noted that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. Here he lists the goods of a simple, renunciant life. He names freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, and a mind that stirs only gently. He asks what generous austerity ripened into this.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You are in a slow, happy season and want to go deeper into it. Bhartrihari wonders at a plain life of freedom, honest food, good company, and learning that brings calm, asking what generous austerity ripened into this. You can let this same wonder meet your garden and your healthy kids today, resting in the dignity you already have rather than grasping for more.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines as a poet who has left behind palace life for a quiet existence by the Ganga. He lists the simple goods of a renunciant: freedom to wander, food eaten without humiliation, noble company, and learning that brings calm. He wonders aloud what generous austerity could have ripened into such a plain life, treating it as a rare blessing rather than a given. You are in a slow, happy season with healthy kids and a growing garden, and you want to savour it without rushing past it.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your boss calling out your mistake in front of everyone has left you feeling like you are of no use. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy and as hard to hold as the wind. When your thoughts keep replaying that moment and refuse to settle, this verse names exactly how stubborn that inner storm can feel.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi as one who treats joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that this difficulty is real, yet practice and letting go can train the mind. Your mind is not broken because it keeps circling that moment at work. It is simply doing what Arjuna named, and it can still be steadied over time.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: When the mind chases a wandering sense, it is swept off like a boat in the wind.
verse_text.translation: When the mind runs after the roving senses, it carries away one's understanding, as the wind carries a boat away on the water.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind chases a wandering sense, it is swept off like a boat in the wind. Your anxious mind keeps replaying the boss calling out your mistake in front of everyone, and one thought pulls it further off course. You do not have to steer against the wind; you can simply notice when the mind has followed the current, and bring your attention back to the oar in your hand right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Like a lamp in a windless place that doesn't flicker: that's a settled mind.
verse_text.translation: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker: that is the image used for the yogi of controlled mind practising union with the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a settled mind is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker. You do not have to force your thoughts flat; you can simply let your attention rest in one place so the flame of your focus stays upright and still gives light. Notice one breath where the air around you feels calm, and let that steadiness be enough for now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Little by little, with patience and steady resolve, settle the mind and let other thoughts go.
verse_text.translation: Little by little one should come to rest, with understanding held steady; fixing the mind on the self, one should think of nothing else.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to settle the mind little by little, with patience and steady resolve, letting other thoughts go. For you, this means the racing thoughts at night do not demand instant silence; calm arrives gradually as you rest your understanding. Tonight, try resting your attention on one steady point, letting the rest drift without forcing it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Yes, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But practice and letting go can train it.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Undoubtedly, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to control. But it is held by practice and by detachment, Kaunteya.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the mind is indeed restless and hard to control, yet it can be held through practice and by loosening its grip. You could try returning your attention to one small task today, then gently letting go of the urge to replay what your boss said. This is not about forcing calm, but about repeatedly coming back and softening what pulls you away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse_text.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.

days.reading: This verse expects the mind to wander. Krishna asks you to bring it back each time it does, gently, without scolding yourself. Every return counts as practice.

story.title: Pingala's song
story.summary: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

days.reading: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who stayed awake listening for a lover who never arrived. She realised her sleeplessness came from hoping someone else would arrive and settle her. You, too, may find that letting go of the hope that someone will fix your restless mind brings the rest that waiting never will.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You have noticed small things bringing you happiness lately, like chai with roommates, a good lecture, and rain, and you want to keep noticing them. The poet Bhartrihari wonders what generous austerity ripened into this freedom to wander, honest food, good company, learning that brings calm, and a mind that stirs only gently. Today, this wonder invites you to see your ordinary student life as a rare blessing rather than taking it for granted.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from his reflection on a simple life. He lists the gifts of a renunciant existence: freedom to move, food eaten with dignity, noble company, learning that ends in calm, and a mind that stays gentle. He wonders what generous austerity could have ripened into such a state. The verse treats these plain goods as a rare blessing, not an ordinary right. Your small moments of peace carry the same weight the poet gives to simple food and quiet study. They are not ordinary background noise.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You sent a slightly sarcastic reply on the team group and have reread it 30 times since. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. In the same way, your thoughts can keep circling that message without your command. The verse names this struggle as real, not a failing, and points toward a steadiness that practice can bring.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi as one who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that this restlessness is real, yet practice and letting go can train it over time. Your mind is circling that reply because it feels exposed. The verse names this circling as real, not a failing, and points toward a steadiness that practice can bring.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: With the divorce papers signed today, a heavy silence has settled in. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else knows this ache; only the heart knows the love it misses. You might find a small relief in naming what is inside you, even if the full weight stays yours alone.
meaning: In the Sundar Kand of the Ramcharitmanas, Ram sends a message to Sita through Hanuman. Sita is captive and has nearly lost hope. Hanuman has just told her Ram's story and dropped his ring from a tree. Now Ram says that speaking of pain lightens it a little. But he asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. The divorce papers signed today have left you in a silence that no one around you can fully enter. Ram's words meet that exact isolation.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You have found time each morning for your Thakurji since retiring, and you want your seva to come from the heart. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those curious, those in need, and the wise. Whatever brought you to this morning routine counts as a worthy door, so your devotion can simply rest in the act of offering itself.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. Whatever brings a person to the search counts as welcome. The verse does not rank them or shut any door. Your morning time with Thakurji began from a place that mattered to you. That origin is already counted among the good. Your seva does not have to earn its right to be heartfelt.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this in the Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures. He holds up the moth and the fish. The moth flies into the flame without knowing it burns. The fish swallows the bait without knowing the hook waits. But we see the danger and still we do not let go. We cling to desires that are tangled in a net of harm. He points out that our delusion runs deeper than simple ignorance. We know the cost and we stay anyway. You sit with this restlessness while your studies wait. The verse names the gap between knowing and stopping, and it does not pretend you are alone in it.

verse_text.speaker: Indra, disguised as a jackal
verse_text.setting: The jackal tells Kashyapa that getting more will not cure his discontent.
verse_text.line: Getting what you want doesn't satisfy. Craving grows like a fire fed with more wood.
verse_text.translation: There is no satisfaction in getting what you want. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes up more, like a fire fed with fuel.

days.reading: Bhishma, through a jackal, says getting what you want brings no satisfaction. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes higher, like a fire fed with fuel. You notice how sweetness draws you in, and each time you break your daily vow, the wanting only grows stronger. Today, watch the fire before you feed it another log.

verse_text.speaker: Yama
verse_text.setting: Nachiketa has refused wealth and long life; Yama begins teaching.
verse_text.line: The good and the pleasant both knock. The wise choose the good; the foolish grab the pleasant.
verse_text.translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them and tells them apart. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.

days.reading: Yama tells Nachiketa that the good and the pleasant both knock at your door, and the wise sift between them while the careless grab what feels nice right now. You reach for something sweet and cannot stop, even after promising yourself otherwise. Today, your task is simply to pause and ask whether what you want is truly good for you or only pleasant in this moment.

verse_text.speaker: Manki
verse_text.setting: Manki, after his last savings are lost in a freak accident, speaks to his own desire.
verse_text.line: Desire, I know your root: my own imagining. I'll stop feeding you, and you'll be gone.
verse_text.translation: Desire, I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all.

days.reading: Manki tells his own desire, 'I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all.' You feel restless while studying, caught in a daily cycle of promising yourself restraint and then breaking it. This points to the moment you picture that next sweet treat and build the wanting in your mind. You can notice that picturing and choose to stop feeding it right there.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
verse_text.translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a steady mind pulls its senses back from what pulls at them, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs. You could try one small tortoise move today: when the pull to scroll or shop rises, close the tab or step back from the screen, then simply notice the pull fade. This is not shutting yourself away, but letting the wanting loosen its grip, just for a moment.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse_text.line: When your mind drifts to harmful things, steer it back to good ones. That's the whole teaching.
verse_text.translation: When the mind has sunk into bad things, bring it down into good ones with effort. That is the summary of all the scriptures.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama: when the mind sinks into harmful things, steer it back to good ones with effort. You could notice when your attention drifts toward what looks sweet, and gently place it on something steady instead. This is not about forcing away a feeling, but about choosing where your mind rests today.

story.title: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
story.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
story.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

days.reading: Manki watches his last money dangle from a camel’s neck until the young bulls die. After blaming fate, he turns to desire itself and names its root as his own imagining, vowing to stop feeding it so it dies. Your daily cycle of promising and breaking feels like that last stake vanishing, yet the story points to the imagining behind the pull, not to fate. Notice where your own imagining takes hold today, and let that image drop.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel like you are no good at anything after your boss points out your mistakes in front of everyone. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and holding it feels like holding the wind. When your thoughts keep replaying those moments at night, you are facing the same restless force Arjuna named, not a personal failing. Notice that force itself, like the wind, without trying to grip it.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard that a steady person sees the joy and pain of all beings as their own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously. It names the mind as a force that resists control. Your boss has singled you out in front of everyone. Now your mind keeps circling that moment. That is the same restless force Arjuna named. It is not proof that you are useless.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the steady yogi who feels all beings as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously. It names the difficulty of steadying the mind rather than denying it. Your mind will not switch off because it is doing what minds do, not because you are failing at rest.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

meaning: Young Rama returns to his father's court after travel. The sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your years of trying and failing have brought you to a place where nothing stirs. This verse meets that numbness directly and treats it as the start of a real question rather than a dead end.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You never imagined your pickle business reaching shops across the state at 58, and you want to keep yourself humble. Bhartrihari wonders at his own freedom to wander, honest food without humiliation, noble company, and a mind that stirs only gently. Today, that same quiet wonder can meet your success: you did not force this, you simply received it, and you can stay open to the calm beneath the achievement.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks from a quiet place by the Ganga, having left behind royal life for a simple existence near Shiva. He lists the gifts of this path, food taken without shame, company of noble people, and learning that brings calm. He asks what generous austerity could have produced such freedom, food, company, and a mind that stirs only gently. Your pickle business reaching shops across the state is a gift that arrived without your forcing it, and this verse invites you to meet that success with quiet wonder rather than pride.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: After twenty years away, you are stepping into a new house and a new routine in India. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. That same energy can meet you now as you begin this chapter, turning the first days of settling in into something you can actually reach.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Ram is overwhelmed by grief after Sita is taken. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her, and his sorrow deepens. Lakshman, Ram's younger brother, pulls him out of despair. He tells him that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the strongest resource a person has, and with it little in the world is unattainable.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You carry mom guilt that feels real. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. This speaks to you today as a question worth sitting with: what is the force behind the choice you keep returning to? You might notice the moment it arises, without letting it define you.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger is the enemy that clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. He tells Arjuna to master this desire rather than let it rule him. Your mom guilt feels real because part of you wants to do right and still falls short. The verse names the pull behind that gap without calling you wicked.
